# Alfred North Whitehead – Concise Summary
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was a British mathematician and philosopher renowned for his contributions to mathematics, logic, philosophy, and education. Educated at Sherborne and Trinity College, Cambridge, he became a fellow at Trinity, teaching and writing on mathematics and physics. Whitehead’s major mathematical works include *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898), *Principia Mathematica* (co-authored with Bertrand Russell, 1910–1913), considered a landmark in mathematical logic, and *An Introduction to Mathematics* (1911), aimed at a general audience. He later shifted focus to philosophy, producing influential works on metaphysics and process philosophy, including *Science and the Modern World* (1925), *Process and Reality* (1929), and *The Concept of Nature* (1920).
Whitehead’s philosophical system, called "process philosophy" or the "philosophy of organism," emphasized reality as composed of interconnected processes and events rather than static, isolated substances. He developed key concepts such as "prehension" (a broad notion of perception affecting all entities) and a novel, dual conception of God that influenced process theology. Whitehead made significant contributions to the philosophy of education, arguing for imaginative, value-laden, and transdisciplinary learning. His ideas have impacted diverse fields, including ecology, economics, biology, physics, and organizational theory. Though admired by major scholars and influential in American progressive theology and Chinese ecological thought, his works remain challenging and are not broadly influential outside specialized circles. Whitehead left no personal archive, making aspects of his life obscure, but his philosophical legacy continues through the efforts of the Whitehead Research Project and various critical editions of his writings.
